paragraphs: I studied abroad for two months at Johns Hopkins University in the United States.

In the first month I did my clerkship in neurosurgery. Hopkins's neurosurgery is simply on a very large scale, with seven to eight operations performed in parallel per day. We gathered at 5 a.m., attended rounds and the residents' study session, and surgery started at 7:30. The daily flow was observing several operations a day and going home in the evening or at night. When I applied for the study abroad I was considering neurosurgery as my future specialty, so I was very much looking forward to what kind of clerkship I could have in an environment blessed with so many cases. In fact, the content of the surgeries was varied, and for brain tumors, in which I am especially interested, I could observe operations nearly every day for meningioma, schwannoma, pituitary adenoma, craniopharyngioma, cerebellar tumors and so on, and I could scrub in for operations in each of the vascular, functional, pediatric and spine areas. What was a little disappointing was that there were almost no opportunities for me to take part by putting my own hands in during surgery. Of course, there are safety issues, so I had expected that the chance of being entrusted with anything from the start was low for a student whose English was even poor, but because it was what I most expected from a clerkship in America rather than Japan, I thought about various ways to improve it. I checked the surgical schedule the day before and tried bombarding the doctors with questions from what I had studied, and tried practising knot tying ostentatiously while waiting. In the end, though, what was valued was not that I had prepared and appealed on my own, but rather, it seemed, the chances for discussion that arose unexpectedly in the outpatient clinic and the ER. I do not know whether the effort paid off, but depending on the doctor, I was allowed to help with wound closure and with processing the skull.

In the second month I did my clerkship in cardiology. Even within cardiology, wards are subdivided by the severity of patients, and I belonged to the team called PCCU, which admits relatively stable patients. It consisted of one attending, one fellow and two residents, and managed about 15 to 20 patients. I arrived at the ward before 8 a.m., did my own rounds, assessed the patients' conditions, drafted proposals for future plans and presented them at the team rounds. There was plenty of time for each patient and the team was small, so I could explain my examination skills and treatment plans without rushing, and I could receive detailed feedback, so it was a very fulfilling clerkship. In the afternoons there was no team schedule, and while the residents did paperwork relentlessly out of the corner of my eye, I spent time freely, observing catheter treatments and cardiac surgery. Gradually I was entrusted with the residents' work. I phoned private practitioners to ask them to send patients' charts, phoned the laboratory to negotiate speeding up a patient's tests, and wrote patients' discharge summaries. The most difficult thing was explaining directly to patients the course of their disease and the content of the tests that would be done. Because I had to explain without using technical terms, it was harder than speaking at conferences and rounds, and I struggled. In clerkships in Japan I had been instructed to answer "I don't know" to patients' questions to avoid trouble, but here a resident always came afterward and corrected me. The patients were also understanding toward students, and I could do my clerkship in a protected environment.

On weekends I made full use of buses and trains to go to nearby cities such as Philadelphia, Washington DC and New York. In particular, the NBA game for which 金君 arranged the tickets was very exciting because it was the playoffs. As for Baltimore itself, the most prosperous seaside area is about the same size as Nagoya Port, and I had the impression that it is a smaller city than I had expected.

To be frank, in the neurosurgery clerkship I only observed even after several weeks and could not do the clerkship I had pictured, and there was a time when I worried that it was because of my own lack of ability. According to a resident, neurosurgery is the department with the least hands-on for students, the authority of the local students was about the same as mine, and when I joined an orthopedic operation I was given a satisfying clerkship despite meeting them for the first time, so I changed my mind, thinking I had been a little unlucky this time. Thinking calmly, the procedures and the content of the work themselves are probably something I can experience once I become a resident, so there may be no need to be that particular about it. More than that, trying various things to be given work, gaining a little trust, and conversely failing and feeling frustrated were very valuable experiences.

Seeing at close range the doctors from the Middle East and South America who were making desperate efforts to produce results, I feel that the greatest advantage of studying abroad while still a student is being free of that kind of pressure. Even if you fail, a chance to make up for it will surely come, and you feel like trying all sorts of things. Through the doctors of the two departments above, I also asked radiology, emergency medicine, cardiac surgery and others to let me do clerkships with them. Every doctor welcomed me without annoyance and made time for me. There is soil here that accepts you if you show interest and draws out new interests.

American hospitals are a connections society. Doctors' letters of recommendation occupy a large place in a resident's employment. During the clerkships I had many experiences of overcoming barriers not through my own effort but through connections with people: when a professor liked me, the treatment I received from the doctors under him changed completely, and in departments where Japanese doctors worked I received more enthusiastic guidance from the surrounding doctors. I was also stimulated by interacting with international students from other countries and other universities whose backgrounds differed from mine. It was a good opportunity to reflect on having spent six years of university in a closed community and to reconsider my future path. I was fortunate to have the chance to notice, before becoming a working adult, that human relationships open up one's view.
Through this study abroad I was given many valuable experiences. I thank everyone who made efforts for me.
